reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / standard medical genetics references
clinicalPearls: Most common sex chromosome aneuploidy in males, caused by one or more extra X chromosomes, typically a 47,XXY karyotype
Often unrecognised until adolescence or adulthood, when hypogonadism and infertility prompt evaluation
Characteristic features include tall stature with long legs, small firm testes, reduced facial and body hair, and gynaecomastia
Testicular failure produces low testosterone with elevated gonadotrophins and, usually, azoospermia
Learning difficulties, particularly with language and executive function, are common though intelligence is usually within the normal range
Testosterone replacement supports pubertal development, bone health, and wellbeing but does not restore fertility
Sperm retrieval techniques can occasionally allow biological fatherhood in selected men
Associated with an increased risk of osteoporosis, metabolic syndrome, venous thromboembolism, and certain tumours
reference.pathophysiology: Klinefelter syndrome results from the presence of one or more supernumerary X chromosomes in a phenotypic male, most commonly a single extra X producing a 47,XXY karyotype, arising from meiotic nondisjunction in either parent. The additional X chromosome material leads to progressive seminiferous tubule fibrosis and hyalinisation, causing primary testicular failure with impaired spermatogenesis and reduced testosterone production, while Leydig cell dysfunction raises luteinising and follicle-stimulating hormone levels. Extra X-linked gene dosage, including genes escaping X-inactivation, is thought to underlie the tall stature, cognitive profile, and other systemic features. Higher-grade aneuploidies produce more severe phenotypes.
additionalInvestigations: Karyotype to confirm the diagnosis and define any mosaicism or higher-grade aneuploidy
Testosterone with luteinising and follicle-stimulating hormone measurement
Semen analysis when fertility is a concern
Bone density assessment given osteoporosis risk
Metabolic screening for glucose intolerance and dyslipidaemia
redFlags: Untreated hypogonadism leading to osteoporosis and fragility fractures
Mediastinal germ cell tumours and a raised risk of male breast cancer
Significant psychosocial and educational difficulties requiring support
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is close to normal, and with testosterone replacement and multidisciplinary support most men lead full lives, though infertility is usual and comorbidity risk is increased.
pitfalls: Delaying diagnosis by attributing tall stature and learning issues to other causes
Overlooking hypogonadism and its long-term skeletal and metabolic consequences
Assuming complete infertility without offering fertility counselling and sperm retrieval options
Not screening for associated metabolic and thromboembolic risks
